description: POLARIS is an engineering-driven team competing in NASA Space Apps 2026. Our goal is to develop an intelligent lunar mission-planning platform that evaluates landing sites, solar energy potential, and Earth communication windows using NASA data. Combining space science, electrical engineering, simulation, AI, and interactive visualization, we aim to transform complex scientific data into practical mission insights.
summary:
POLARIS is an interactive lunar mission decision-support prototype developed for NASA Space Apps 2026. It helps users understand how landing-site location, terrain, illumination, and mission delays affect operations near the Moon's south pole.

Using NASA/JPL Horizons ephemerides and NASA LOLA topography, POLARIS compares two reference locations and three mission scenarios, visualizing Sun and Earth visibility alongside photovoltaic generation, electrical demand, battery state of charge, and potential energy shortfalls.

Its engineering Copilot interprets supported natural-language questions and translates them into reproducible simulations. Users can explore alternative electrical configurations, evaluate mission constraints, and generate evidence-based reports.

POLARIS brings space science and electrical engineering into one accessible platform while explicitly documenting the limitations of its preliminary models.
details:
The Problem

Exploring the Moon's south pole presents important scientific and engineering challenges. Low solar elevations, uneven terrain, and changing observation geometry affect local sunlight, Earth visibility, and the availability of electrical energy. Mission delays may alter these conditions and create new operational constraints.

Although NASA provides valuable planetary datasets, combining topography, observation geometry, and power-system analysis into an understandable decision-making workflow remains challenging.

Our Solution: POLARIS

POLARIS is an interactive lunar mission decision-support prototype that integrates NASA planetary observations with engineering simulations.

The application provides eight interconnected workspaces: Mission, Sky & Terrain, Scenarios, Power Systems, Lunar Atlas, Evidence, AI Copilot, and Decision Review.

Users can compare two reference locations near the lunar south pole, examine local Sun and Earth visibility, simulate mission delays, evaluate alternative observation sites, and generate engineering reports.

Electrical Engineering Contribution

POLARIS introduces a preliminary photovoltaic and battery energy feasibility model.

The system estimates solar power generation using solar geometry, modeled visibility, panel area, efficiency, and orientation. It then calculates electrical consumption, battery state of charge, and potential unmet energy over the simulated mission period.

Users can modify photovoltaic array area, electrical demand, and battery capacity to investigate engineering trade-offs and identify configurations with improved energy margins.

A conceptual electrical architecture connects solar generation, power conversion, DC distribution, battery storage, and mission loads. Detailed converter design and electrical protection calculations remain future work.

Engineering Copilot

The POLARIS Copilot interprets supported natural-language engineering questions and converts them into numerical simulation requests.

For example, a user can request a 40% increase in electrical demand and obtain recalculated mission scenarios, energy constraints, and battery performance estimates.

Numerical results originate from the deterministic Python scientific engine, rather than from generative AI predictions. The prototype does not currently depend on a connected external language model.

NASA Data and Scientific Validation

POLARIS integrates NASA/JPL Horizons ephemerides, NASA GSFC LOLA lunar topography, NASA Moon Trek mapping resources, and LROC QuickMap.

NASA NAIF SPICE was also used for independent consistency checks of the astronomical geometry, including 228 angular comparisons.

The application was developed using Python, FastAPI, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, GitHub, and Vercel.

Innovation and Impact

POLARIS combines lunar observation geometry with preliminary electrical power feasibility and explainable decision support in one publicly accessible platform.

Its educational and engineering value lies in helping users understand the consequences of changing mission schedules, observation locations, electrical loads, and storage assumptions.

Rather than producing an unsupported claim about the safest landing location, POLARIS shows the constraints, evidence, and trade-offs behind each modeled scenario.

Limitations

POLARIS is an engineering demonstration, not a flight-qualified mission-planning system.

Its local terrain model covers a 6 km horizon, its reference observations are sampled at six-hour intervals, and its simplified electrical model does not include detailed thermal behavior, converter dynamics, battery degradation, or certified protection design.

Earth visibility above the local skyline does not establish actual radio communication availability.

Future improvements include detailed electrical-system modeling, multi-objective optimization, higher-resolution simulations, and further scientific validation.
